html:
The learning problem confronting the brain is remarkable not only in scale but in heterogeneity. The system must simultaneously acquire hierarchical generative models of high-dimensional sensory streams, calibrate precise sensorimotor transformations requiring millisecond-scale temporal fidelity, discover behavioral policies that maximize reward over horizons ranging from seconds to years, and encode episodic records of individual experiences with sufficient specificity to support one-shot inference. These demands impose fundamentally different constraints on learning rate, memory persistence, representational format, and error signal structure. A fast learning rate that enables single-trial memorization of an episode would be catastrophic for the slow, interleaved statistical learning needed to extract stable sensory representations 1, 2, 3. The cerebellum’s comparatively explicit teaching channel (climbing fibers) supports rapid calibration and timing-sensitive prediction learning–classically framed as supervised error-driven learning, but now understood to include broader predictive and outcome-related teaching signals 4, 5, 6–whereas cortical learning is often hypothesized to rely more on locally generated self-supervised/predictive errors under modulatory gating. No single set of plasticity parameters can satisfy these demands simultaneously. The model proposes a biological mapping of message passing (Figure) 52.

Throughout this section, an optimizer refers to any neural circuit motif that repeatedly implements the following loop:

Propose: generate internal activity patterns representing predictions, candidate actions, or inferred latent causes. A 2026 model examines distributed predictive processing (Figure) 53.

Compare: evaluate those proposals against constraints (sensory observations, motor outcomes, rewards and punishments, social feedback, homeostatic set points), producing an error-like signal–a message that reflects the discrepancy, though not necessarily in the form of an explicit gradient 7. A 2026 model compares error-neuron microcircuits with predictive-coding networks (Figure) 54.

Assign credit: attribute the mismatch to particular parameters–often only approximately, locally, or with substantial temporal delay 8. A 2025 mouse study measures dopamine signals consistent with action prediction errors (Figure) 55.

Update: modify synaptic weights, intrinsic excitability, or network structure so that future proposals better satisfy the constraints 9, 10. A 2025 hippocampal-slice study tests synaptic tagging and capture (Figure) 56.

Not every system implements each step with equal fidelity or explicitness. The cerebellum’s climbing-fiber-driven complex spikes provide a comparatively explicit instructive channel that supports rapid calibration and relatively precise credit assignment, classically framed as supervised error-driven learning but now known to carry broader predictive and outcome-related teaching signals 4, 11, 12, 6. In contrast, the basal ganglia’s dopaminergic signal is a low-bandwidth, temporally sparse broadcast that conveys value- and outcome-prediction errors, requiring synaptic eligibility traces and three-factor learning rules to bridge temporal gaps between action and feedback 13, 14, 8. The hippocampus emphasizes rapid associative binding rather than incremental optimization: novelty and mismatch signals bias the system toward encoding, while dendritic plateau potentials enable large, single-trial synaptic updates (BTSP) that support one-shot learning; nevertheless, hippocampal subfields–particularly CA1–exhibit match-mismatch / mnemonic prediction-error responses that may regulate when memories are written or updated 15, 16, 17. These differences in how the optimization loop is realized–and where it is approximate, compressed, or bypassed–are among the most informative features of the brain’s learning architecture. Climbing-fiber stimulation can substitute for the air puff during mouse eyeblink conditioning (Figure).

The brain’s solution is to partition the learning problem across multiple, anatomically distinct optimization systems, each embodying inductive biases appropriate to its subdomain. Doya influentially formalized this decomposition by mapping three major brain systems onto machine learning paradigms 18: the cerebral cortex performs unsupervised learning through redundancy reduction and self-organization; the cerebellum performs supervised learning using climbing fiber signals from the inferior olive as explicit teaching inputs 19, 20, 21; and the basal ganglia perform reinforcement learning using dopaminergic reward prediction errors–classically characterized as a scalar signal, but increasingly consistent with a heterogeneous, multi-dimensional teaching signal: population diversity can be interpreted in distributional-RL terms (different neurons behaving like different "optimism/expectile" channels), and dopamine responses can also reflect prediction errors about specific task variables / sensory features, with the effective dimensionality depending on which projection/striatal subnetwork reads the signal out 22, 23, 24. In predictive-coding / predictive-processing accounts 25, 7, 26, 27, the cortical paradigm is now more accurately described as self-supervised–the cortex generates its own targets by predicting incoming input and learns from structured, high-dimensional prediction errors propagated across its hierarchical layers 28. To these three systems, the hippocampal formation adds a fourth optimizer: a fast, one-shot relational memory system that binds conjunctions of cortical activity patterns into retrievable episodes through behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity and Hebbian auto-association 29, 1, 17, 30. The analysis shows how hippocampal reinstatement was measured (Figure) 57.

This four-system decomposition is not merely a pedagogical convenience–it reflects deep differences in neural architecture, connectivity, cell-type composition, and plasticity mechanisms, all of which have been detailed in the preceding systems-level sections. Table 1 summarizes the key computational characteristics of each optimizer. Several features of this landscape deserve emphasis. Granule and climbing-fiber signals can be imaged together (Figure) 58.

The brain’s four major optimization systems compared across key computational dimensions. Abbreviations: CF = climbing fiber; IO = inferior olive; PF = parallel fiber; PC = Purkinje cell; RPE = reward prediction error.
Cerebral Cortex Cerebellum Basal Ganglia Hippocampus
Learning paradigm Self-supervised/predictive Supervised Reinforcement One-shot relational binding
Error / teaching signal Cortical prediction errors (hierarchical, feedback-mediated) Climbing fiber signals (IO) Phasic dopamine RPEs (VTA/SNc); distributional and feature-aware Novelty / mismatch; dendritic plateau potentials
Signal format Structured, high-dimensional, topographic Structured, temporally precise Compressed at the synapse; population-/projection-structured Sparse, conjunctive
Routing Point-to-point cortical feedback connections Point-to-point synaptic (IO→\toCF→\toPC) Broad neuromodulatory projections with topographic organization (projection-specific readouts) (Mostly) local circuit (EC→\toHPC→\toEC)
Primary update rules Hebbian, STDP, homeostatic; neuromodulator-gated (3-factor) PF->PC LTD/LTP + plasticity in deep nuclei (and intrinsic plasticity) Three-factor (pre×\timespost×\timesDA) BTSP, Hebbian LTP
Learning timescale Slow-dominant (statistical, across sessions) with fast adaptation in some regimes Fast-moderate (across trials) Moderate (across episodes) Fast (single exposure)
What is learned World model, perceptual and conceptual representations Forward models, timing, calibration Policies, value functions, habits Episodes, relational/cognitive maps

First, the error signals driving these systems differ not only in what they encode but in bandwidth, format, and routing, which strongly constrains what each system can learn. In predictive-coding / predictive-processing accounts, cortex relies on high-dimensional, topographically organized error-like signals generated by hierarchical feedforward/feedback interactions, providing rich information about what and where predictions failed for updating generative models 25, 28. Cerebellar learning is distinguished by an explicit instructive channel: climbing-fiber events from the inferior olive deliver sparse but powerful, temporally precise teaching signals (classically framed as error-driven supervision, though their content can be broader than simple motor error) 31, 32, 4. By contrast, basal ganglia learning is driven by dopamine as a compressed neuromodulatory teaching signal: dopamine responses are heterogeneous across neurons/projections and are consistent with distributional/value 22 and task-variable (feature) prediction-error components 23, 33, but any given synapse effectively receives a low-bandwidth modulatory factor–so temporal/synaptic credit assignment depends heavily on eligibility traces and repetition 8, 34. Finally, hippocampal rapid encoding emphasizes gated one-shot storage: novelty/mismatch can control "write" state, and dendritic plateau potentials drive BTSP over behavioral timescales (seconds), enabling episodic traces to form in a single pass through experience 17.

Second, these four optimizers do not operate in isolation. In the online loop, cortex supplies rich state representations and prediction errors, while basal ganglia and cerebellum sit in parallel cortico-subcortical-thalamo-cortical loops that act on cortical activity as well as plasticity: basal ganglia implement a value-weighted gating/selection mechanism that stabilizes chosen cortical action plans into habits under dopaminergic teaching, whereas cerebellum provides fast forward-model predictions and temporally precise error-corrective feedback that refines ongoing control and can serve as an instructive signal for cortical (and downstream) representations 18, 4, 13, 8. The hippocampus complements these incremental learners by binding episodes and latent context, then re-injecting that context into cortex (to condition inference) and into striatum (to disambiguate state and sharpen credit assignment), with dopamine additionally coupling systems by regulating both striatal updates and hippocampal encoding "write" policies 1, 15. Coordination is then achieved by (i) neuromodulatory meta-control, which sets a brain-wide learning regime (plasticity gain, exploration/arousal mode, encoding-retrieval bias) appropriate to uncertainty and utility 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, and (ii) replay-mediated inter-system teaching, where hippocampal sharp-wave ripple replay–coordinated with neocortical slow oscillations/spindles and modulated by reward circuitry–trains slower cortical models while also imprinting value-sensitive regularities into striatum and motor circuits 41, 42, 43, 44.

Third, the multi-optimizer architecture entails a system-level arbitration problem: when systems produce conflicting behavioral recommendations, control is typically allocated gradedly via reliability- (and effort-) weighted meta-control rather than an all-or-nothing switch. Along with the emergent competitive dynamics that pervade the entire brain, computational theory and human neuroimaging support an uncertainty-based scheme in which each controller tracks the reliability of its predictions from recent state/reward prediction errors, and an inferior lateral PFC/frontopolar-rostral cingulate arbitration circuit adjusts their mixture weights–down-weighting dorsolateral striatal / posterior putamen model-free valuations when model-based predictions are reliable, but reverting toward cached/habitual control when deliberative models become unreliable or too costly 45, 46, 47, 48. This arbitration is modulated by neuromodulatory and hormonal state, but the updated picture is nuanced: acute stress effects on goal-directed vs habitual balance show substantial task- and individual-dependent boundary conditions (with mixed replications), whereas chronic/recent stress history more consistently disrupts action-outcome learning and promotes inflexible habits via identified amygdala-striatal pathways 49, 50, 51.

The remainder of this section examines each of these optimization systems in detail (characterizing its error signals, learning rules, and the nature of the representations it acquires) before turning to the inter-system coordination mechanisms that bind the ensemble into a coherent learning architecture.

Browse by system and aspect

Each system is written up the same way: what it optimizes, the error signals that drive it, how those signals change synapses, and the learning that results.
